In brief, intracellular parasites were incubated with mouse anti-GRA1 (at 1:500 dilution) or mouse anti-GRA2 (at 1:500 dilution) and rabbit anti-HA antibodies (for TgVMPAIDHA, at 1:200 dilution), followed by incubation with appropriate secondary antibodies (Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated F(ab’) donkey anti-rabbit IgG and Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated F(ab’) donkey anti-mouse IgG) and DAPI (10µg/ml). The cells were observed for GRA1 and GRA2 localization patterns under 100× objective of the Zeiss LSM 880 confocal laser scanning microscope, images were acquired in Airyscan mode using Zen Black software, and processed using ImageJ software. Maximum intensity projections of z-stack images were obtained using z-projection of ImageJ software. ≥50 PVs were examined for the presence of GRA1 and GRA2 localization patterns, and the experiment was repeated three times. The number of PVs with IVN was presented as a percentage of the total number of PVs observed using GraphPad Prism.

To determine biogenesis of dense granules, purified -IAA and +IAA tachyzoites were added on poly-L-lysine-coated slides, and processed for IFA using mouse anti-GRA1 (at 1:500 dilution) or mouse anti-GRA2 (at 1:500 dilution) antibodies, followed by incubation with appropriate secondary antibodies (Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated F(ab’) donkey anti-mouse IgG) and DAPI (10µg/ml). The cells were observed under the 100× objective of the Olympus FV3000 confocal laser scanning microscope, and images were captured using Fluoview FV31S-SW software. For super-resolution images, cells were observed under the 100× objective of the Zeiss LSM 880 confocal laser scanning microscope, and images were acquired in Airyscan mode using Zen Black software. Images were processed using ImageJ software. The fluorescence signal intensity of GRA1 or GRA2 in each tachyzoite was measured using the Multi Measure option of the ROI manager, and calculated using the formula “IntDen-(Area of interest×mean signal intensity of the background)”. The mean signal intensity of +IAA parasites was plotted as a percentage of the mean signal intensity of -IAA parasites (% Signal intensity) based on multiple -IAA (n=338) and +IAA (n=383) parasites from three independent experiments. The cells were also analyzed for intraparasitic distribution of GRA1 or GRA2 signal, and the number of parasites with perinuclear accumulation of GRA1 or GRA2 signal was presented as a percentage of the total number of parasites observed using GraphPad Prism.

For co-localization of dense granules with ER-GFP, RHTIR1-VMP1AID::ER-GFP parasites were cultured with 0.1% ethanol (-IAA) or 500µM IAA (+IAA) as has been described in the “Effect of TgVMP1 depletion on gliding motility” section, tachyzoites were purified, and processed for IFA as described in the “VMP1 localization” section using mouse anti-GRA1 (at 1:500 dilution) or mouse anti-GRA2 (at 1:500 dilution) and rabbit anti-GFP antibodies (for ER-GFP, at 1:200 dilution), followed by incubation with appropriate secondary antibodies (Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated F(ab’) donkey anti-rabbit IgG and Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated F(ab’) donkey anti-mouse IgG) and DAPI (10µg/ml). The cells were observed under a 100× objective of the Zeiss LSM 880 confocal laser scanning microscope, images were acquired in Airyscan mode using Zen Black software, and processed using ImageJ software.

Effect of TgVMP1 depletion on lipid droplets
RHTIR1-VMP1AID parasites were cultured with 0.1% ethanol (-IAA) or 500µM IAA (+IAA) as has been described in the “Effect of TgVMP1 depletion on gliding motility” section, tachyzoites were purified, stained with Nile red (250ng/ml in complete DMEM) at 37 ⁰C for 30min, washed with PBS, and observed for fluorescence (λex=488 nm, λem=530 nm) under 100× objective of the Zeiss LSM 880 confocal laser scanning microscope, images were acquired using Zen Black software, and processed using ImageJ software. The number of lipid droplets (LDs) was determined and presented as the number of LDs/parasite using GraphPad Prism. We also measured the surface area (µm2) of each LD using the analyze particles option of ImageJ software, and presented it as mean LD size (μm2) using GraphPad Prism.

Immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry
For immunoprecipitation of TgVMP1AIDHA, RHTIR1 and RHTIR1-VMP1AID parasites were cultured without IAA for 48h post-invasion, as has been described in the “Parasite culture” section. The purified tachyzoite pellets were resuspended in 300µl of lysis buffer (10mM Tris, 150mM NaCl, 5mM EDTA, 0.1% NP-40, 10% glycerol, 1× protease inhibitor cocktail, pH 7.5), incubated for 30min on ice with intermittent mixing, sonicated using Bioruptor for 5min (30s On/30s Off at high amplitude), and the lysates were incubated for 30min in ice. The lysates were centrifuged at 4°C for 15min at 20,000×g, and the supernatants were collected. The pellets were again extracted with 150µl of lysis buffer as described above, and supernatants were pooled with the respective first supernatant. The supernatant was incubated with 5µg of rabbit anti-HA antibodies for 12h at 4°C, mixed with protein A/G magnetic beads (10µl slurry/2mg of protein) for 2h at 4°C, and washed with lysis buffer. The beads were washed with lysis buffer, mixed with an equal volume of 2× SDS-PAGE sample buffer, incubated at 99°C for 10min, and the supernatant was collected as an eluate. Aliquots of input, flow through, wash, and eluate were processed for western blotting using mouse anti-HA antibodies (1:1000 dilution), followed by goat HRP-conjugated anti-mouse antibodies (1:20,000 dilution), as has been described in the “VMP1 expression” section. The remaining eluate was subjected to mass spectrometry analysis.

The immunoprecipitates were run on a 12% SDS-PAGE gel until the protein size ladder completely entered the gel. The protein-containing region was excised and processed for trypsin digestion and peptide extraction as has been described previously81,82. The peptide solution was run on Q Executive HF (Thermo Scientific) for HCD mode fragmentation and LC-MS/MS analysis. The raw data were imported into the Proteome Discoverer 2.2 software (Thermo Scientific), and proteins were identified by searching against the T. gondii RH-88 Uniprot databases using the SEQUEST HT algorithm. The analysis parameters included trypsin enzyme specificity, a maximum of two missed cleavages, variable modifications, such as carbamidomethylation of cysteine, oxidation of methionine, and deamidation of asparagine/glutamine. Precursor tolerance was set to 5 ppm, and fragmentation tolerance was set to 0.05 Da. Peptide spectral matches (PSM) and peptide identifications grouped into proteins were validated using the Percolator algorithm and filtered to a 1% false discovery rate (FDR). The peptide abundances in RHTIR1 and TgVMP1AIDHA immunoprecipitates from three biological repeats were compared for enrichment analysis using MetaboAnalyst 6.0 (https://www.metaboanalyst.ca/) with a single-factor statistical analysis. Imputation was done by replacing missing values with 1/5th of the minimum positive value of each variable, and normalization was performed based on the sum of the abundances. The abundance value was transformed to Log10, and the auto-scaling option was used for data scaling. Proteins enriched ≥1.5-fold with a p-value<0.05 in TgVMP1AIDHA immunoprecipitate compared to the RH-TIR1 immunoprecipitate were considered significant interactors of TgVMP1.

Scramblase assay
TgVMP1AIDHA and PfVMP1AIDHA proteins were purified from RHTIR1-VMP1AID and PfVMP1AID parasites, respectively, as described in the “Immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry” section. Briefly, the parasite lysate supernatants were incubated with HA-Trap magnetic agarose beads (ChromoTek; 25µl beads for 2mg/ml protein) for 12h at 4°C. The beads were washed (wash buffer: 20mM Tris, 500mM NaCl, 0.03% n-dodecyl β-D-maltoside (DDM), pH 7.4), and the bound proteins were eluted in 150µl elution buffer (25mM Tris, 150mM NaCl, pH 7.4) with HA peptide (0.64mg/ml). The eluate was diluted ~100 fold with storage buffer (20mM Tris, 150mM NaCl, 0.03% DDM, 5% glycerol and 1× protease inhibitor cocktail, pH 7.4), concentrated to ~50µl using Amicon Ultra centrifugal filter (10 kDa cut-off) at 4°C, flash frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80°C until further use. Aliquots of input, flow through, washes, and eluate fractions were checked for the presence of TgVMP1AIDHA or PfVMP1AIDHA proteins by western blotting using rabbit anti-HA antibodies (at 1:1000 dilution), followed by goat HRP-conjugated anti-rabbit antibodies (1:20,000 dilution) as has been described in the “VMP1 expression” section.

Liposomes were prepared as has been reported previously22,99. In brief, POPC, POPS, and NBD-PS were dissolved in chloroform. POPC and POPS were mixed at 9:1 molar ratio along with 0.4 mol% NBD-PS. The lipid mixture was dried in a glass bottle under a nitrogen stream to form a uniform layer, followed by vacuum drying at room temperature for 12h. The dried lipid layer was rehydrated using rehydration buffer (50mM HEPES, 100mM NaCl, pH 7.5) to obtain multilamellar vesicles (MLVs) at a final concentration of 10.5mM. MLVs were subjected to 10 rounds of freeze-thaw cycles and diluted in rehydration buffer to 5.25mM. The sample was passed 21 times through a 0.4µm filter, followed by 11 times through a 0.2µm filter using a mini extruder (Avanti Polar Lipids) to obtain uniform-sized liposomes. The liposomes were stored at 4°C until further use.

Scramblase assay was performed as has been described previously22,99. Liposomes (5.25mM) were destabilized by mixing with DDM (0.36% w/v final), and the mixture was incubated at room temperature for 3h at 10 rpm on a nutator. The destabilized liposomes were mixed with storage buffer (with 0.36% DDM) or purified proteins (TgVMP1AIDHA or PfVMP1AIDHA in storage buffer with 0.36% DDM) at a 2:1 ratio (v/v) to prepare empty-liposomes or proteoliposomes (TgVMP1-liposomes or PfVMP1-liposomes), respectively. The samples were incubated at room temperature for 1.5h to allow protein incorporation into the liposomes. DDM was removed by incubating the samples serially with 25mg Bio-Beads for 1h at room temperature, 25mg Bio-Beads for 2h at room temperature, and 50mg Bio-Beads for overnight at 4°C. The liquid phase containing liposomes was separated and diluted to 200µM using rehydration buffer. 50µl of the empty or proteoliposome sample was transferred to a 96-well flat-bottom white polystyrene plate, and assessed for fluorescence signal (λex=470 nm, λem=530 nm) using the SpectraMax iD3 multi-mode microplate reader (Molecular Devices). The fluorescence signal intensity was measured at every 26s interval for 208s, followed by dithionite (10mM final concentration) for 416s, and then with Triton X-100 (0.5% (w/v)) for 208s. Relative fluorescence intensities of empty and proteoliposomes were calculated for each time point, and plotted as (Ft - FTriton)/(F0 - FTriton), where Ft is the fluorescence intensity at the corresponding time point, F0 is the initial fluorescence intensity, and FTriton is the fluorescence intensity after addition of Triton X-100 (at the 208s time point). The relative fluorescence intensity was plotted on the y-axis over time on the x-axis using GraphPad Prism.

Expression of PfVMP1 and HsVMP1 in RHTIR1-VMP1AID parasites
A synthetic and mammalian-codon optimized PfVMP1 coding sequence (PfVMP1syn) was amplified from the pUC-PfVMP1syn plasmid using PfVMP1-Frec/PfVMP1-R primers. The T. gondii tubulin promoter region was amplified from pCTG-Fluc plasmid using TgTub-F/TgTub-PfVMP1-Rrec primers100. The PfVMP1-Frec and TgTub-PfVMP1-Rrec primers contain overlapping sequences, which allowed recombination of PfVMP1syn and tubulin promoter fragments by PCR using TgTub-F/PfVMP1-R primers. The recombined PCR product was digested with PacI/AvrII and cloned into similarly digested pMyc3×.LIC-DHFR plasmid to obtain pTub-PfVMP1syn-3×Myc-DHFR plasmid. A synthetic and T. gondii-codon-optimized HsVMP1 coding sequence (HsVMP1syn) was cloned into pJET1.2/Blunt vector, excised with EcoRV/AvrII, and subcloned into similarly digested pTub-PfVMP1syn-3×Myc-DHFR plasmid to obtain pTub-HsVMP1syn-3×Myc-DHFR plasmids. 15µg of pTub-PfVMP1syn-3×Myc-DHFR or pTub-HsVMP1syn-3×Myc-DHFR plasmid was transfected into RHTIR1-VMP1AID parasites as has been described in the “Generation of recombinant T. gondii parasites” section. The transfected parasites were selected with 1µM pyrimethamine without IAA until the resistant parasites emerged. The resistant parasites with pTub-PfVMP1syn-3×Myc-DHFR plasmid (RHTIR1-TgVMP1AID::PfVMP1Myc) would express PfVMP1Myc, and the resistant parasites with pTub-HsVMP1syn-3×Myc-DHFR plasmid would express HsVMP1Myc. These parasites were cultured with 0.1% ethanol (-IAA) or 500µM IAA (+IAA). The parasite lysates were evaluated for expression of TgVMP1AIDHA (rabbit anti-HA antibodies), PfVMP1Myc or HsVMP1Myc (mouse monoclonal anti-Myc antibodies at 1:1000 dilution), and SAG1 (mouse anti-SAG1 antibodies) as a loading control by western blotting, as has been described in the “VMP1 expression” section. The RHTIR1-TgVMP1AID::PfVMP1Myc and RHTIR1-TgVMP1AID::HsVMP1Myc parasites were assessed for co-localization of TgVMP1AIDHA with PfVMP1Myc or HsVMP1Myc, respectively, by IFA as has been described in the “VMP1 localization” section. The parasites were incubated with mouse anti-Myc (at 1:200 dilution) and rabbit anti-HA antibodies (for TgVMP1, at 1:200 dilution), followed by appropriate secondary antibodies (Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated F(ab’) donkey anti-rabbit IgG and Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated F(ab’) donkey anti-mouse IgG) and DAPI (10µg/ml). The cells were observed under a 100× objective of the Zeiss LSM880 confocal laser scanning microscope, images were acquired in Airyscan mode using Zen Black software, and processed using ImageJ software. Pearson’s correlation coefficient for co-localization was determined using the JACoP plugin in Fiji.

To study whether PfVMP1Myc or HsVMP1Myc complement the growth of TgVMP1-depleted parasites, the parental RHTIR1-VMP1AID and complemented (RHTIR1-TgVMP1AID::PfVMP1Myc, RHTIR1-TgVMP1AID::HsVMP1Myc) parasites were grown without (–IAA) or with (+IAA) IAA, and compared for overall growth by plaque assay and intracellular development by replication assay as has been described in the “Effect of TgVMP1 depletion on parasite growth” section. Plaques were observed using the 1× objective at 40× digital zoom of AXIO Zoom.V16 microscope, and images were taken using the Zen Blue software.

To evaluate whether PfVMP1Myc or HsVMP1Myc can rescue the dense granule biogenesis defect, the parental RHTIR1-VMP1AID and complemented (RHTIR1-TgVMP1AID::PfVMP1Myc, RHTIR1-TgVMP1AID::HsVMP1Myc) parasites were grown without (–IAA) or with (+IAA) IAA, and compared for localization of dense granule protein GRA2 as has been described in the “Effect of TgVMP1 depletion on IVN formation, and dense granule secretion and biogenesis” section.

Intracellular calcium monitoring
RHTIR1-VMP1AID parasites were cultured without (-IAA) or with (+IAA) IAA for 14h, and tachyzoites were purified as described in the “Parasite culture” section. The parasites were evaluated for intracellular calcium levels using Fluo-4 AM as has been described previously101. The purified parasites were washed with Ringer’s solution (10mM HEPES, 2mM CaCl2, 1mM MgCl2, 4.5mM KCl, 155mM NaCl, 10mM D-glucose, pH 7.4), incubated with 250nM of Fluo-4 AM for 10min, washed with and resuspended in Ringer’s solution, transferred to poly-L-lysine-coated glass slides, and observed under the 100× objective of Olympus FV3000 confocal microscope. Images were acquired using Fluoview FV31S-SW software, the fluorescence signal intensity/tachyzoite was measured using the Multi Measure option of the ROI manager of ImageJ software, and calculated using the formula “IntDen-(Area of interest×mean signal intensity of the background)”. Multiple parasites from three independent experiments were observed, and the mean signal intensity/parasite of +IAA parasites was presented as a percentage of the mean signal intensity/parasite of -IAA parasites using GraphPad Prism.

Transmission electron microscopy
RHTIR1-VMP1AID parasites were cultured with 0.1% ethanol (-IAA) or 500µM IAA (+IAA) as has been described in the “Effect of TgVMP1 depletion on gliding motility” section. Intracellular parasites were processed for transmission electron microscopy (TEM) as has been previously described102. Briefly, parasites were washed with 0.1M phosphate buffer (PB, pH 7.4) and fixed (PB with 2.5% glutaraldehyde and 2% paraformaldehyde) overnight at 4°C. The fixed cells were scraped off, washed with PB, incubated in 1% osmium tetroxide (in PB) for 1h at room temperature, washed twice with distilled water, stained en bloc with 2% aqueous uranyl acetate for 1h, and washed twice with distilled water. The sample was dehydrated using increasing percentages of ethanol (30%, 70%, 80%, 90%, and 95%) for 10min each, followed by three treatments with 100% ethanol for 15min each. The sample was infiltrated with epoxy and ethanol mixtures (1:3 for 2h, 1:1 for 12h, and 3:1 for 3h) at room temperature. This was followed by sequential incubations in 100% epoxy resin for 3h, 12h, and 3h. The cells were transferred to 100 % epoxy and polymerized at 62⁰C for 72h. Ultrathin sections (50–70nm thickness) were cut using an ultramicrotome (Ultracut UCT; Leica Microsystems) using a glass knife. These sections were transferred onto a 200 mesh copper grid, air-dried, and stained with uranyl acetate and lead citrate for 5min each. These sections were visualized using a Talos L120C transmission electron microscope operating at 120kV, and imaged using 4k×4k Ceta CMOS camera. Images were acquired and processed using Velox software.

Immunoelectron microscopy
RHTIR1-VMP1AID parasites were cultured with 0.1% ethanol (-IAA) or 500µM IAA (+IAA) as has been described in the “Effect of TgVMP1 depletion on gliding motility” section. Immunoelectron microscopy (IEM) of intracellular parasites was performed essentially as previously described102. Briefly, cells were washed with 0.1M phosphate buffer (PB), fixed (PB with 4% paraformaldehyde and 0.1% glutaraldehyde) for 15min at room temperature, followed by fresh fixative for 2h at 4°C. The cells were scraped off, washed with PB, dehydrated sequentially using increasing percentage of ethanol (30%, 50%, 70%, 80%, 90%, and 95%) for 10min each, and then dehydrated twice with absolute ethanol for 15min each. The cells were incubated twice in ethanol-LR white mixture (1:1) for 1h each with a change of the mixture. The cells were incubated in 100% LR white for 8h at 4°C, followed by incubation in 100% LR white for 2h at room temperature, and incubated at 55°C for 72h to polymerize. Ultrathin sections (50–70nm) were cut using an ultramicrotome and transferred onto nickel-coated grids. The grids were quenched with 50mM NH₄Cl (in PB) for 10min and blocked (2% skimmed milk in PBT (PB with 0.05% Tween-20)) for 1h at room temperature. The grids were incubated with mouse anti-ROP1, anti-GRA2 or anti-MIC2 antibodies (1:20 dilution in PBT with 3% BSA) for overnight at 4°C without agitation, washed with PBT, incubated with 6nm gold-conjugated goat-anti-mouse IgG antibodies (1:20 dilution in PBT with 3% BSA) for 1h, and washed with PBT. The grids were post-fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde for 10min, washed with distilled water, stained with uranyl acetate, washed again with distilled water, and air-dried. The sections were imaged as described above in the “Transmission electron microscopy” section.

We evaluated GRA2 secretion by extracellular parasites with modification of a previously described method103. Briefly, RHTIR1-VMP1AID parasites were cultured with 0.1% ethanol (-IAA) or 500µM IAA (+IAA) as has been described in the “Effect of TgVMP1 depletion on gliding motility” section. 5×103 purified tachyzoites (in 10μl DGH medium) were placed onto a glow-discharged carbon-coated 200-mesh nickel grids, and allowed to glide for 15min at room temperature. Excess solution was gently wicked off, the grids were fixed with 1% paraformaldehyde for 10min, and probed with anti-mouse-GRA2 primary antibodies (1:20 dilution), followed by 6nm gold-conjugated anti-mouse IgG (1:20 dilution) as has been described above for ultrathin sections. Gold particles localized in the vicinity of each parasite were counted and presented as the number of particles/1µm² area of the micrograph.

Effect of TgVMP1 depletion on apicoplast
RHTIR1-VMP1AID parasites were cultured with 0.1% ethanol (-IAA) or 500µM IAA (+IAA) as has been described in the “Effect of TgVMP1 depletion on gliding motility” section, and assessed for the presence of apicoplast by IFA using antibodies to acyl carrier protein (ACP) as has been described in the “VMP1 localization” section. The infected cells were incubated with rabbit anti-ACP (at 1:500 dilution) and mouse anti-HA (at 1:200 dilution) antibodies, followed by incubation with appropriate secondary antibodies (Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated F(ab’) donkey anti-rabbit IgG, Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated F(ab’) donkey anti-mouse IgG) and DAPI (10µg/ml). The cells were observed under the 100× objective of the Olympus FV3000 confocal laser scanning microscope, and images were acquired using Fluoview FV31S-SW software and processed using ImageJ software. Maximum intensity projections of z-stack images were obtained using the Z-projection of the ImageJ software. At least 150 parasites were observed to determine apicoplast/nucleus ratio in each of the three independent experiments, and data were plotted using GraphPad Prism.

Statistical analysis
The significance of the difference between the two groups was determined by using a two-tailed Student’s t-test, and the p-values are mentioned in the respective figure legends.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This paper entitled « An ER-resident lipid scramblase is crucial for biogenesis and function of apicomplexan parasite secretory organelles » by G. Srinivas Reddy et al describes the important role of the vacuole membrane protein 1 (VMP1), a DedA superfamily member of T. gondii (TgVMP1). They showed that PfVMP1 and TgVMP1 are ER-localized lipid scramblases. While none of their attempts to knock down PfVMP1 worked in P. falciparum, TgVMP1 depletion adversely affected parasite development, motility, host cell invasion, and egress. These phenotypes were linked to impaired rhoptry and dense granule biogenesis, and decreased secretion of micronemes in TgVMP1-depleted parasites, indicating a crucial role forTgVMP1. TgVMP1 depletion impaired lipid droplet homeostasis and ER organization. They rescued the ER-localized lipid scramblase by complementing TgVMP1-depleted parasites with PfVMP1 or a homolog as distant as human VMP1 rescued the depleted parasites, indicating their functional conservation and a crucial role for ER- resident lipid scramblase activity in the biogenesis and function of secretory organelles.
The manuscript is well written and the experiments were correctly designed and well-conducted. Therefore, I will recommend its publication after a minor revision. The data generated are almost convincing, except the comments below.
The quality of this can be improved by answering the following concerns.
1) The authors wrote at the end of the abstract, the following sentence : « The essentiality of TgVMP1 for parasite development and likely functional conservation of apicomplexan VMP1 proteins highlight their drug-target potential ». This is unnecessary because it not convincing at all that PfVPM1 and TgVPM1, which are so conserved with the distant human counterpart and this later can perfectly complement the TgVPMM1 mutant, can be used for a drug-target design. Otherwise, the authors should tell how this can happen. I will suggest to remove this kind sentence, which have no true added value.
2) The authors do not discuss why all attempts in P. falciparum to knock down PfVPM1 do not work at all whereas there is no difficulty to genetically disrupt the function of TgVPM1 in T. gondii. What is the reason ? This is surprising since TgVPM1 and PfVPM1 are the same multilayer tarnsmembrane proteins in these both closely related apicomplexan parasites.
3) They authors indicate several times that TgVPM1 is involved in the biogenesis of rhoptries and dense granules while it is not implicated in microneme biogenesis. The data provided to reach this conclusion are not convincing because only confocal microscopy and few antibodies have used to perform these experiments. An immuno-electron microscopy (IEM) using few antibodies specific to rhoptries, micronemes and dense granules should be used to see the subcellular distribution of gold-particules on these organelles. IEM will also demonstrate whether these proteins are properly located in the space destination after secretion.
4) The authors indicate that the secretion of ROP proteins are disturbed while ROP1 protein appears nicely and more concentrated in the PVM in the mutants relative to the parental parasites when carefully looking at the images provided. It will be more convincing to perform serial ultrathin sections in only one chosen small vacuole containing few intracellular parasites to obtain several images that will be superimposed to reconstitute the whole bodies of the mutants and parental parasites. These experiments will allow to determine whether they are less rhoptries in the mutants versus the wild type parasites because these organelles will be counted. The number of rhoptries in mutants vers wild type parasites may impact the level of protein secretion. In addition, this experimental strategy will show if the mutant parasites still have distal and basal micronemes because a negative impact in their distributions in the apical end of the parasites may also explain why there is an effect on their secretion.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Here, the authors described in Toxoplasma and Plasmodium a lipid scramblase, the vacuole membrane protein 1 (VMP1), that they nicely showed to be associated with ER in both parasites. They present a range biochemical, ultrastructural and experimental cell biological data, to interrogate the role of Toxoplasma VMP1. They showed that parasites have a strong defect in replication, motility and invasion, that is associated with a defect in the biogenesis of their secretory organelles dense granules and rhoptries. Moreover, TgVMP1 depletion impaired lipid droplet homeostasis and ER organization, a phenotype that can be rescued with PfVMP1 or human VMP1.
The characterization of DedA-like protein in apicomplexa is novel. In other organisms, the cellular abnormalities observed due to the loss of VMP1 are multiple: fragmented ER, ER-contact, distorted Golgi, impaired endocytosis and exocytosis, damaged mitochondria, and accumulation of ubiquitinated-protein aggregates and lipid droplets (LDs)… Here the authors focused only on the biogenesis of secretory organelles and lipid droplets accumulation. The characterization of the secretory organelles in the mutant is incomplete. A full analysis is needed to better assess the importance of this DedA-predicted protein in parasites. Overall structural details of the mutant are missing and the interpretation of some results is confusing.
1. The authors performed TEM but the images shown do not allow drawing any conclusion because the poor preservation of the material : no intracellular membranes can be seen and therefore, ER and Golgi cannot be observed. This is particulary important for ER, since they claimed a change in the localisation of ER marker in the mutant (Figure S9). While they showed a strong defect in dense granules secretion, they do not analyze if dense granules are visible by TEM in the mutant ; they only focused on rhoptries. TEM should also resolves if micronemes are properly formed and present at the apex, including lateral micronemes, and sub-conoid micronemes. The analysis by IFA is not sufficient. Overall, the ultrastructure of the mutant by TEM is not conclusive and cannot support the claimed drawn by IFA, in particular, analysis of ER, dense granules, mitochondria.
2. The authors overlook the fact that the parasite has a very serious replication defect. 75% of vacuoles contains a single parasite. This can be explained by the absence of dense granule proteins secretion, which was recently shown to be important for intracellular parasite development (Chelaghma et al. ELife 2024 ; Fu et al. PloS Pathogen 2023). However, the phenotype of replication is more drastic than in any of the mutants of annuli defective for secretion of dense granules (Chelaghma et al, eLife 2024 ; Fu et al., PlosPathogen 2023) or biogenesis of secretory organelles (Morlon-Guyot et al., Cell Mic 2015 ; Sloves et al. Cell Host microbes, 2012). This might suggest a role of lipid droplets homeostasis in growth, or potential other overlooked effects (point 1).
3. Since DedA is important in autophagosomes formation and that PI3K, ATG8, ATG3… are linked to Apicoplast in Apicomplexa, the presence and inheritence of the apicoplast during division need to be assessed.
4. The phenotype related to dense granules is parcelar. We would like to see further investigation of whether or not they are formed (TEM, see above). If they are visible, then to quantify secretion in more details (release in the media by quantification of GRAs in the ESA). The loss of IVM is suggested in TEM but the authors cannot quantify the association of GRA proteins with IVN by IFA (Fig 6B and S8B), we can just say that they are or not in vacuolar space. Association with IVN required specific fractionnation procedures.
5. IFA figure 5A. The authors say that the rhoptries are fragmented. The resolution of IFA do not permit to see details of the morphologies of the rhoptries, even to see individual rhoptries. The ROP1 signal seems to be in the vacuolar space upon depletion of TgVMP1. First this should be confirmed by adding phase contrast. Second, the release of rhoptry proteins within the lumen is already observed upon depletion of proteins involved in rhoptry biogenesis (SORTILIN, VPS11, retromer complex…), and this is not discussed. Why there is still important signal in -IAA in panel 5A ?
6. GRASP-GFP staining is weird ; it normally looks like a bar above the nucleus near the ER. I don’t think that they can use these images to claim colocalisation with Golgi.
7. The authors observed a strong defect in motility, secretion of micronemes and rhoptries. Since most of the parasites are not able to divide, it might be difficult to distinguish between a potential defect in parasite gliding motility vs. parasites that are dead or dying and thereby are unable to exhibit active motility. Same for microneme and rhoptry secretion assays.
8. Some of the results deserve more discussion.
-Any explanation of why dense granules proteins but not rhoptry proteins accumulated at the ER in the mutant ?
-VMP1 is an ER-resident protein so is expected to play a role in this compartment. Since the three secretory organelles, micronemes, rhoptry and dense granules, transit through the ER, why only dense granules and rhoptries are affected ? MICs proteins may follow, at some level, a different trafficking pathway ?
-it is surprising to see that 50% of mice survived after infection with the mutant (+IAA) while there is no plaques at all in vitro. The authors should comment on this discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo.
9. The interpretation of mass spectrometry data are questionable. The authors performed three independ IPs, but do not show any statistical significance of the enrichment, that will help for the conclusions, especially because almost all the proteins that they used to make their point are not enriched in the three sets of data. This is not clear how they connect an association of VMP1 with these proteins (MICs, GRAs, ROPs, IMC proteins) and biogenesis of secretory organelles.
10. The authors referred to the absence of network when they look at IFA of dense granule proteins. The IVN is not visible by IFA.
11. Fig. S4A. For the fusion of miniAID in Plasmodium, did the authors control by WB the expression of Tir1 in the transgenic line, which is a prerequisite for this conditional KD ?
12. Section PfVMP1 and TgVMP1 localize to ER. ‘Towards characterization of apicomplexan VMP1 proteins, we replaced wild-type PfVMP1 and TgVMP1 coding sequences …’ This is not replacement of gene but endogenous tagging.
13. Figure S2 : Molecular sizes of PCR products on schematic and gels are missing.
14. Table : add accession number TGGT1

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
RESPONSES TO THE REVIEWER COMMENTS
Below are our responses to the reviewers’ comments in a point-wise manner. The comments
are italicized and excerpts from the manuscript are highlighted with the page No. and line No.
corresponding to the start of excerpt in the file “Reddy, et al_Revised Manuscript”.
REVIEWER #1
Comment 1. The authors wrote at the end of the abstract, the following sentence: The
essentiality of TgVMP1 for parasite development and likely functional conservation of
apicomplexan VMP1 proteins highlight their drug-target potential. This is unnecessary…..I
will suggest to remove this kind sentence…...
Response. As suggested, we have removed the sentence “The essentiality of TgVMP1 for parasite development and likely functional conservation of apicomplexan VMP1 proteins highlight their drug-target potential” from the abstract on page 2.
Comment 2. The authors do not discuss why all attempts in P. falciparum to knock down
PfVPM1 do not work at all whereas there is no difficulty to genetically disrupt the function of
TgVPM1 in T. gondii. What is the reason ? This is surprising since TgVPM1 and PfVPM1 are
the same multilayer tarnsmembrane proteins in these both closely related apicomplexan
parasites.
Response: We were also surprised with the failure of PfVMP1 knock-down in P. falciparum.
We have discussed this point in the text on page 8, line 191: “…..It is possible that intrinsic
nature and ER membrane localization of PfVMP1 rendered it refractory to degradation
in case of cDD and glmS systems, as has also been reported for other proteins 44,45. The
auxin-inducible knock-down was quite effective for TgVMP1 in T. gondii but not for
PfVMP1 in P. falciparum, which might be due to differences in the specificity of E3 ligases
of P. falciparum and T. gondii for TIR1. Similar to our observation, previous studies
showed limited success of the auxin-inducible system in P. falciparum 45. ”.
Comment 3. The authors indicate several times that TgVPM1 is involved in the biogenesis of
rhoptries and dense granules while it is not implicated in microneme biogenesis. The data
provided to reach this conclusion are not convincing because only confocal microscopy and
few antibodies have used to perform these experiments. An immuno-electron microscopy (IEM)
using few antibodies specific to rhoptries, micronemes and dense granules should be used to
see the subcellular distribution of gold-particules on these organelles. IEM will also
demonstrate whether these proteins are properly located in the space destination after
secretion.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion, and agree that confocal
microscopy alone would not provide a complete picture of the secretory organelles. We have
performed extensive TEM and IEM experiments to assess the effect of TgVMP1 depletion of
micronemes, rhoptries, and dense granules. The TEM data are in agreement with the IFA data,
and IEM data showed labelling of organelles with the corresponding marker protein-specific
gold particles. The new figures and related results have been incorporated in the text as
described below for each organelle:
Micronemes. Page 14, line 349: “Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images
confirmed the presence of both apical and lateral micronemes in +IAA and –IAA
parasites (Supplementary Fig. 6C), which was also corroborated by MIC2 labelling in
immunoelectron microscopy (IEM) images (Supplementary Fig. 7A). Furthermore, the
TEM micrographs showed comparable number of apical micronemes in –IAA
(9.9±5.9/apical region, n=22 parasites) and +IAA (9.0±4.4/apical region, n=22 parasites)
parasites, which together with the IFA data indicate that TgVMP1 depletion did not
affect microneme organization.”.
Rhoptries. Page 17, line 396: “……For rhoptry organization, intracellular +IAA and –
IAA tachyzoites were processed for IFA, TEM, and IEM. IFA images showed ROP1
localization to characteristic rhoptry-like elongated structures with a bulbous base in the
majority (85.3%) of -IAA parasites as compared with only a small number (11.3%) of
+IAA parasites (Fig. 5A, B). Similar to the intracellular parasites, purified -IAA parasites
also exhibited ROP1 localization to rhoptry-like elongated structures, which was not the
case with +IAA parasites (Fig. 5E). In agreement with the IFA data, TEM images showed
apical rhoptries in 52.2% of -IAA parasites (n=23 parasites), whereas only 18.2% of +IAA
parasites had apical rhoptries (n=22 parasites) (Fig. 5F). ROP1 labelling of the similar
structures in IEM micrographs indicated ROP1 targeting to these structures
(Supplementary Fig. 7B)”.
Dense granules. Page 20, line 483: “….TEM micrographs of both –IAA and +IAA
parasites showed dense granules (Fig. 5F, 6C), which was corroborated by IEM showing
GRA2 labelling of dense granules in the parasite cytoplasm and IVN in the PV
(Supplementary Fig. 7C). The TEM micrographs of +IAA parasites contained less
number of cytoplasmic dense granules (1.5/parasite section, n=153) than those of –IAA
parasites (3.2/parasite section, n=94), which together with the IFA data indicates a crucial
role of TgVMP1 in dense granule biogenesis. We next compared dense granule secretion
in the ESA of purified –IAA and +IAA parasites by IEM using GRA2. The number of
GRA2-gold particles was comparable (Supplementary Fig. 7D, E), suggesting that
impaired dense granule biogenesis did not affect secretion. Nonetheless, majority of the
gold particles were associated with electron dense material in –IAA parasites as opposed
to +IAA parasites (Supplementary Fig. 7D), suggesting a defect in the post-secretion
process that might be required for the formation of IVN.”.
Comment 4. The authors indicate that the secretion of ROP proteins are disturbed while ROP1
protein appears nicely and more concentrated in the PVM in the mutants relative to the
parental parasites when carefully looking at the images provided. It will be more convincing
to perform serial ultrathin sections in only one chosen small vacuole containing few
intracellular parasites to obtain several images that will be superimposed to reconstitute the
whole bodies of the mutants and parental parasites. These experiments will allow to determine
whether they are less rhoptries in the mutants versus the wild type parasites because these
organelles will be counted. The number of rhoptries in mutants vers wild type parasites may
impact the level of protein secretion. In addition, this experimental strategy will show if the
mutant parasites still have distal and basal micronemes because a negative impact in their
distributions in the apical end of the parasites may also explain why there is an effect on their
secretion.
Response: The reviewer’s comment is valuable, and we have addressed it below in a), b), and
c).
a). ROP1 protein appears nicely and more concentrated in the PVM in the mutants relative to
the parental parasites when carefully looking at the images provided.
Response. Indeed, ROP1 signal appears to be predominant in the PV of +IAA parasites as
compared to that of -IAA parasites, suggesting abnormal secretion. Nonetheless, in contrast to
the –IAA parasite, ROP1 signal does not localize to characteristic rhoptry-like elongated
structures in the +IAA parasites, indicating their absence. We have revised our analysis and
determined the number of +IAA and –IAA parasites with typical rhoptry-like elongated
structures (Fig. 5A, B) or diffuse ROP1 signal in the PV (Fig. 5C, D). The results are described
on page 17, line 397 (“…IFA images showed ROP1 localization to characteristic rhoptry-
like elongated structures with a bulbous base in the majority (85.3%) of -IAA parasites
as compared with only a small number (11.3%) of +IAA parasites (Fig. 5A, B). 59.4% of
+IAA parasites also showed ROP1 signal in the PV compared to 10.9% of -IAA parasites
(Fig. 5C, D).…”).
b). It will be more convincing to perform serial ultrathin sections in only one chosen small
vacuole containing few intracellular parasites to obtain several images that will be
superimposed to reconstitute the whole bodies of the mutants and parental parasites. These
experiments will allow to determine whether they are less rhoptries in the mutants versus the
wild type parasites because these organelles will be counted. The number of rhoptries in
mutants vers wild type parasites may impact the level of protein secretion.
Response. We could not obtain serial ultrathin TEM sections corresponding to the same
parasite to reconstruct a 3D image. Nonetheless, we carried out fresh TEM and IEM
experiments, and added new data in support of the defects in secretory organelles in TgVMP1-
depleted parasites, which is mentioned above in response to comment 3.
We also performed super-resolution Airyscan microscopy with 100 nm Z-slices,
followed by 3D reconstruction of ROP1 labelling in –IAA and +IAA parasites. As evident from
the below figure, the mutant parasites (+IAA) do not have typical elongated rhoptries.
Accessory Fig. 1A. 3D reconstruction of ROP1 localization. -IAA and +IAA RHTIR1-
VMP1AID parasites were evaluated for rhotpry organization by IFA using anti-ROP1
antibodies. Super-resolution Airyscan micrographs of the whole PVs were acquired using Zeiss
LSM 880 confocal laser scanning microscope under the 100× objective with 100 nm optical
sections. The representative 3D reconstructed Airyscan image shows rhoptries (magenta) and
nucleus DAPI (cyan) in a PV with 4 parasites. Note that ROP1 signal is restricted to
characteristic rhoptry-like elongated structures in -IAA parasites, as compared with
predominantly disordered structures in +IAA parasites. Scale bar = 5 µm.
We could not count the number of rhoptries/parasite using the above 3D reconstruction
images, as IFA does not offer the resolution required to distinguish individual rhoptries.
Moreover, the number of rhoptries is variable in Toxoplasma, and it would also vary from
section to section of the TEM images observed. Hence, we determined the number of parasites
with apical rhoptries in mutant and control parasites, and it is included on page 17, line 402
(“……..In agreement with the IFA data, TEM images showed apical rhoptries in 50% of
-IAA parasites (n=24 parasites), whereas only 13.6% of +IAA parasites had apical
rhoptries (n=22 parasites) (Fig. 5F). ROP1 labelling of the similar structures in IEM
micrographs indicated ROP1 targeting to these structures (Supplementary Fig.
7B)…...…..”).
c). In addition, this experimental strategy will show if the mutant parasites still have distal and
basal micronemes because a negative impact in their distributions in the apical end of the
parasites may also explain why there is an effect on their secretion.
Response. We performed super-resolution Airyscan microscopy with 100 nm optical sections,
followed by 3D reconstruction of MIC2 labelling in –IAA and +IAA parasites. The image
shown below indicates that both the parasites contain apical and lateral micronemes.
Accessory Fig. 1B. 3D reconstruction of MIC2 labelling. -IAA and +IAA RHTIR1-
VMP1AID parasites were evaluated for microneme organization by IFA using anti-MIC2
antibodies. Super-resolution Airyscan micrographs of the whole PVs were acquired using Zeiss
LSM 880 confocal laser scanning microscope under the 100× objective with 100 nm optical
sections. The representative 3D reconstructed Airyscan image shows localization of MIC2 in
a PV with 2 parasites. Note MIC2 labelling in apical (A) and lateral (L) regions of both the
+IAA and -IAA parasites, indicating the presence of apical and lateral micronemes. Scale bar
= 2 µm.
The above 3D reconstruction data is consistent with the IFA (Fig. 4A-D), TEM (Supplementary
Fig. 6C), and IEM (Supplementary Fig. 7A) data, which show both apical and lateral
micronemes in mutant and control parasites (page 14, line 347: “……All these proteins
showed similar predominant apical localization in +IAA and –IAA parasites, ruling out
any adverse effect of TgVMP1 in microneme organization (Fig. 4A-D; Supplementary
Fig. 6A, B). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images confirmed the presence of
both apical and lateral micronemes in +IAA and –IAA parasites (Supplementary Fig.
6C), which was also corroborated by MIC2 labelling in immunoelectron microscopy
(IEM) images (Supplementary Fig. 7A). Furthermore, the TEM micrographs showed
comparable number of apical micronemes in –IAA (9.9±5.9/apical region, n=22 parasites)
and +IAA (9.0±4.4/apical region, n=22 parasites) parasites, which together with the IFA
data indicate that TgVMP1 depletion did not affect microneme organization.”).
We have not included the Accessory Fig. 1A and B in the text, as the included TEM
micrographs offer better appreciation of rhoptries and micronemes in mutant vs control
parasite. However, if desired by the reviewer, we will be glad to include these figures along
with videos (uploaded on the portal) in the main text.
Reviewer #2
Comment 1. The authors performed TEM but the images shown do not allow drawing any
conclusion because the poor preservation of the material : no intracellular membranes can
be seen and therefore, ER and Golgi cannot be observed. This is particulary important for
ER, since they claimed a change in the localisation of ER marker in the mutant (Figure S9).
While they showed a strong defect in dense granules secretion, they do not analyze if dense
granules are visible by TEM in the mutant ; they only focused on rhoptries. TEM should also
resolves if micronemes are properly formed and present at the apex, including lateral
micronemes, and sub-conoid micronemes. The analysis by IFA is not sufficient. Overall, the
ultrastructure of the mutant by TEM is not conclusive and cannot support the claimed drawn
by IFA, in particular, analysis of ER, dense granules, mitochondria.
Response: We greatly appreciate reviewer’s suggestions. As suggested, we performed fresh
experiments for TEM and IEM, and scanned several micrographs to evaluate the effects of
TgVMP1 depletion quantitatively on secretory organelles. We have included brand new TEM
and IEM micrographs and related results in the text as mentioned below.
Micronemes: Page 14, line 349: “Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images
confirmed the presence of both apical and lateral micronemes in +IAA and –IAA
parasites (Supplementary Fig. 6C), which was also corroborated by MIC2 labelling in
immunoelectron microscopy (IEM) images (Supplementary Fig. 7A). Furthermore, the
TEM micrographs showed comparable number of apical micronemes in –IAA
(9.9±5.9/apical region, n=22 parasites) and +IAA (9.0±4.4/apical region, n=22 parasites)
parasites, which together with the IFA data indicate that TgVMP1 depletion did not
affect microneme organization.”.
Rhoptries. Page 17, line 396: “……For rhoptry organization, intracellular +IAA and –
IAA tachyzoites were processed for IFA, TEM, and IEM. IFA images showed ROP1
localization to characteristic rhoptry-like elongated structures with a bulbous base in the
majority (85.3%) of -IAA parasites as compared with only a small number (11.3%) of
+IAA parasites (Fig. 5A, B). Similar to the intracellular parasites, purified -IAA parasites
also exhibited ROP1 localization to rhoptry-like elongated structures, which was not the
case with +IAA parasites (Fig. 5E). In agreement with the IFA data, TEM images showed
apical rhoptries in 52.2% of -IAA parasites (n=23 parasites), whereas only 18.2% of +IAA
parasites had apical rhoptries (n=22 parasites) (Fig. 5F). ROP1 labelling of the similar
structures in IEM micrographs indicated ROP1 targeting to these structures
(Supplementary Fig. 7B)”.
Dense granules. Page 20, line 483: “….TEM micrographs of both –IAA and +IAA
parasites showed dense granules (Fig. 5F, 6C), which was corroborated by IEM showing
GRA2 labelling of dense granules in the parasite cytoplasm and IVN in the PV
(Supplementary Fig. 7C). The TEM micrographs of +IAA parasites contained less
number of cytoplasmic dense granules (1.5/parasite section, n=153) than those of –IAA
parasites (3.2/parasite section, n=94), which together with the IFA data indicates a crucial
role of TgVMP1 in dense granule biogenesis.”.
LD. Page 22, line 536: “…TEM micrographs confirmed the presence of much larger size
LDs in +IAA parasites than in -IAA parasites (Fig. 7D), indicating a key role for TgVMP1
in LD homeostasis. Additionally, LDs were closely associated with ER membrane in +IAA
parasite, which was not evident in –IAA parasites.”.
ER. Page 24, line 585: “..ER-GFP was prominently clustered around the nucleus in a
significant number of +IAA parasites (Fig. 7E, F). TEM micrographs showed ER tubules
stretched throughout the +IAA parasites, including in close contact with LDs, whereas
these were mostly perinuclear in –IAA parasites. These data indicate impaired ER
organization..”.
The method sections related to TEM and IEM have been revised as well (page 57-59).
Comment 2. The authors overlook the fact that the parasite has a very serious replication
defect. 75% of vacuoles contains a single parasite. This can be explained by the absence of
dense granule proteins secretion, which was recently shown to be important for intracellular
parasite development (Chelaghma et al. ELife 2024 ; Fu et al. PloS Pathogen 2023). However,
the phenotype of replication is more drastic than in any of the mutants of annuli defective for
secretion of dense granules (Chelaghma et al, eLife 2024 ; Fu et al., PlosPathogen 2023) or
biogenesis of secretory organelles (Morlon-Guyot et al., Cell Mic 2015 ; Sloves et al. Cell Host
microbes, 2012). This might suggest a role of lipid droplets homeostasis in growth, or potential
other overlooked effects (point 1).
Response: We thank the reviewer for bringing up this point to our notice. We agree that the
replication defect upon TgVMP1 depletion is more severe than that has been reported in case
of dense granule defect (Chelaghma, et al., 2024 (reference No. 66 in the text); Fu, et al., 2023
(reference No. 67 in the text)) or micronemes and rhoptries (Sloves, et al. 2012 (reference No.
56 in the text; Stasic, et al. 2029 (reference No. 57 in the text)). We acknowledge reviewer’s
point that this severe replication defect upon TgVMP1 depletion could be a combined result of
defects in secretory organelles and LD homeostasis. We have discussed this point on page 32,
line 808 (“…The accumulation of enlarged LDs in close association with ER membrane
in TgVMP1-depleted parasites indicates impaired LD homeostasis, which together with
impaired secretory organelle biogenesis could have contributed to the overall block of
parasite growth..…”).
The other potential reasons for severe parasite growth defect are discussed on page 32,
line 790 (“…Additionally, as IVN formation requires lipids from the host as a primary
source and parasite as a secondary source 9,65, impaired lipid homeostasis in TgVMP1-
depleted parasites could have limited lipid supply to the PV, thereby, adversely affecting
IVN formation and parasite growth…”), page 32, line 806 (“…..ER-resident lipid
scramblase activity is crucial for parasite development, which likely functions via
translocation of lipids in the ER and the precursor vesicles destined to the secretory
organelles………..This further indicates that the loss of ER-localized lipid scramblase
activity is the major reason for impaired secretory organelle biogenesis, ER organization,
LD homeostasis, and IVN formation in TgVMP1-depleted parasites, consequently
blocking the parasite development. ”),
Comment 3. Since DedA is important in autophagosomes formation and that PI3K, ATG8,
ATG3… are linked to Apicoplast in Apicomplexa, the presence and inheritence of the
apicoplast during division need to be assessed.
Response: Indeed, human VMP1 has been shown to be required for autophagy during early
stages (references 28 and 29). As suggested, we addressed this point by comparing -IAA and
+IAA parasites for the presence of apicoplast using antibodies to the apicoplast marker protein
ACP. We did not observe any noticeable difference in the presence of apicoplast across the
number of –IAA and +IAA parasites observed, which has been mentioned on page 33, line
822: “….HsVMP1 recruits the PI3K complex (VPS34/Beclin 1/Vps15) at the phagophore
assembly site via interaction with Beclin 1, which is crucial for autophagosome formation
28,29. A striking consequence of the ablation of autophagy pathway in T. gondii and P.
falciparum has been shown to be the loss of apicoplast, a relict plastid that produces fatty
acid precursors 70. We compared TgVMP1-depleted and control parasites for the
presence of apicoplast as a marker to assess whether TgVMP1 depletion affected
autophagy. The proportion of apicoplast-containing TgVMP1-depleted and control
parasites was comparable (Supplementary Fig. 12), suggesting that the observed
phenotypes of TgVMP1-depleted parasites are not associated with autophagy-related
defects.”.
Comment 4. The phenotype related to dense granules is parcelar. We would like to see further
investigation of whether or not they are formed (TEM, see above). If they are visible, then to
quantify secretion in more details (release in the media by quantification of GRAs in the ESA).
The loss of IVM is suggested in TEM but the authors cannot quantify the association of GRA
proteins with IVN by IFA (Fig 6B and S8B), we can just say that they are or not in vacuolar
space. Association with IVN required specific fractionnation procedures.
Response: This is a valid point, and we thank the reviewer for prompting us to further address
the effect of TgVMP1 depletion on dense granule biogenesis, secretion, and IVN formation.
As has been described in response to comment 1, we have included brand new TEM and IEM
data related to the effect of TgVMP1 depletion on dense granule biogenesis and IVN formation.
The related excerpts from result and discussion sections are mentioned below.
Page 20, line 483: “….TEM micrographs of both –IAA and +IAA
parasites showed dense granules (Fig. 5F, 6C), which was corroborated by IEM showing
GRA2 labelling of dense granules in the parasite cytoplasm and IVN in the PV
(Supplementary Fig. 7C). The TEM micrographs of +IAA parasites contained less
number of cytoplasmic dense granules (1.5/parasite section, n=153) than those of –IAA
parasites (3.2/parasite section, n=94), which together with the IFA data indicate a crucial
role of TgVMP1 in dense granule biogenesis.. …”.
We agree with the reviewer that IFA images showing diffuse GRA signal do not
indicate loss of IVN. It was a misinterpretation on our part, and we have revised the concerned
result section on page 19, line 467 (“….The number of parasites with diffuse GRA1 or
GRA2 localization was significantly higher in +IAA parasites (83.6% for GRA1, 79.0%
for GRA2) than that in –IAA parasites (9.6% for GRA1, 14.6% for GRA2) (Fig. 6B;
Supplementary Fig. 8B). TEM images showed the absence of tubulo-vesicular IVN in the
PV of 57.7% +IAA parasites (n=123 PVs) as compared with 7.8% –IAA parasites (n=64
PVs) (Fig. 6C), indicating a crucial role for TgVMP1 in IVN formation.”).
We quantified GRA2-gold particles as a measure of dense granule secretion in ESA
by IEM. The results are mentioned on page 20, line 488 (“…..We next compared dense
granule secretion in the ESA of purified –IAA and +IAA parasites by IEM using GRA2.
The number of GRA2-gold particles was comparable (Supplementary Fig. 7D, E),
suggesting that impaired dense granule biogenesis in TgVMP1-depleted parasites did not
affect secretion. Nonetheless, majority of the gold particles were associated with electron
dense material in –IAA parasites as opposed to +IAA parasites (Supplementary Fig. 7D),
suggesting a defect in the post-secretion process that might be required for the formation
of IVN.”).
Our IFA, TEM, and IEM data are consistent with each other, and show defects in dense
granule biogenesis, post-secretion assembly of dense granule-secreted proteins, and IVN
formation, which are discussed on page 31, line 775 (“…..TgVMP1-depleted parasites
contained less number of dense granules and also showed accumulation of dense granule
proteins in the ER. The impaired ER organization in TgVMP1-depleted parasites might
have affected the transport and assembly of dense granule proteins during transport
through the ER/Golgi endo-membrane system, thereby, causing their accumulation in
ER. Although fewer, the cytoplasmic dense granules in TgVMP1-depleted parasites
showed normal secretion……………Both control and TgVMP1-depleted parasites
secreted comparable GRA2 in the ESA. However, in contrast to TgVMP1-depleted
parasites, majority of the GRA2 was associated with electron dense material in the ESA
of control parasites………….This suggests a defect in the form of secreted-GRA2 or post-
secretion assembly of GRA2 that might be necessary for IVN formation,
…………………as IVN formation requires lipids from the host as a primary source and
parasite as a secondary source 9,67, impaired lipid homeostasis in TgVMP1-depleted
parasites could have limited lipid supply to the PV, thereby, adversely affecting
IVN formation and parasite growth. .…..”).
Comment 5. IFA figure 5A. The authors say that the rhoptries are fragmented. The resolution
of IFA do not permit to see details of the morphologies of the rhoptries, even to see individual
rhoptries. The ROP1 signal seems to be in the vacuolar space upon depletion of TgVMP1.
First this should be confirmed by adding phase contrast. Second, the release of rhoptry proteins
within the lumen is already observed upon depletion of proteins involved in rhoptry biogenesis
(SORTILIN, VPS11, retromer complex…), and this is not discussed. Why there is still important
signal in -IAA in panel 5A ?
Response: Once again, thank you for bringing up these valid points to our notice, which we
inadvertently missed or misinterpreted. Certainly, IFA doesn’t offer the resolution required to
count individual rhoptries and assess rhoptry morphology. Accordingly, we have corrected the
y-axis label of Fig. 5B, which now reads as: “%Parasites with normal rhoptries”. We have
also rephrased the concerned sentence on page 17, line 400: “..Similar to the intracellular
parasites, purified -IAA parasites also exhibited ROP1 localization to rhoptry-like
elongated structures, which was not the case with +IAA parasites (Fig. 5E)…..”).
We have added Fig. 5C with phase contrast to show ROP1 signal in the PV and
determined the numbers of PVs with ROP1 signal (Fig. 5D), as mentioned on page 17, line 399
(“….59.4% of +IAA parasites also showed ROP1 signal in the PV compared to 10.9% of
-IAA parasites (Fig. 5C, D)…..”). We have discussed this result on page 31, line 766 (“…the
loss of apical rhoptries and secretion of ROP1 in the PV of TgVMP1-depleted parasites
are similar to those observed in parasites with ablation of TgSORTLR, V-type proton
ATPase or Vps11 56,57,65. It is possible that TgVMP1 contributes to rhoptry biogenesis via
interaction with TgSORTLR and V-type proton ATPase, and loss of this interaction in
TgVMP1-depleted parasites could have adversely affected rhoptry biogenesis...”).
The faint signal in the “VMP1” panel of +IAA parasites in the previous Figure 5A could
have been due to incomplete TgVMP1 depletion. However, it doesn’t impact the result, as we
have evaluated at least 100 PVs from each of the 3 independent experiments to quantitate the
effect of TgVMP1 on rhoptries (Fig. 5B). We have replaced this panel in the revised manuscript
with a better representative image.
Comment 6. GRASP-GFP staining is weird ; it normally looks like a bar above the nucleus
near the ER. I don’t think that they can use these images to claim colocalisation with Golgi.
Response: We agree with the reviewer that GRASP-GFP localizes to a bar-like structure above
the nucleus (Bisio, et al., 2020; Palletier, et al. 2002). We repeated the experiment to check
whether TgVMP1 colocalizes GRASP-GFP. Indeed, we also observed that GRASP-GFP
localization is predominantly bar-like close to the nucleus. We have revised Fig.1F, and
mentioned the related result in the text on page 6, line 146 (“….We episomally expressed ER-
GFP or GRASP-GFP in RHTIR1-VMP1AID parasites, which showed substantial co-
localization of ER-GFP with TgVMP1AID (Fig. 1E, F), indicating that TgVMP1 is
HA
present in ER. On the other hand, only a minor proportion of TgVMP1 co-localized with
GRASP-GFP in the region proximal to ER…….”).
Comment 7. The authors observed a strong defect in motility, secretion of micronemes and
rhoptries. Since most of the parasites are not able to divide, it might be difficult to distinguish
between a potential defect in parasite gliding motility vs. parasites that are dead or dying and
thereby are unable to exhibit active motility. Same for microneme and rhoptry secretion assays.
Response: This is a valid and important comment. To address whether the observed defects
could be due to parasite death, we set up the experiment exactly as been described in the method
section “Effect of TgVMP1 depletion on gliding motility” on page 46, and performed
propidium iodide (PI) staining of purified parasites as an indicator of cell death (Accessory Fig.
2A). As shown in the below Accessory Fig. 2B, the -IAA and +IAA parasites showed similar
viability, indicating that the observed defects in motility, invasion, and organelle secretion are
not due to the presence of dead parasites in the sample used in related experiments.
Accessory Fig. 2. Viability of parasites. RHTIR1-VMP1AID parasites were cultured with
0.1% ethanol (-IAA) or 500 µM indole-3-acetic acid (+IAA) as has been described in the
“Effect of TgVMP1 depletion on gliding motility” section. Purified -IAA and +IAA parasites
were incubated with PI (5 μg/ml in PBS) for 15 min at room temperature, washed with PBS,
immediately observed under the 100 objective of Zeiss Axioimager.Z2 fluorescence
microscope, images were acquired using AxioVision software, and analysed using ImageJ
software. A. The representative micrographs show PI staining (PI), DIC, and merge of the two
panels (Merge). Scale bar = 10 µm. PI staining indicates cell death. B. The number of PI-
negative -IAA and +IAA parasites in “A” was counted and presented as a percentage of the
total number of parasites observed (% Viable parasites) on y-axis for the indicated parasites on
x-axis. Each data is from 2 independent experiments (-IAA, n=324 cells; +IAA, 452 cells). The
significance of difference between two data sets is indicated (ns: not significant).
We have not included this figure in the text, as there are already 8 main figures and 13
supplementary figures. Nonetheless, we have included the result on page 13, line 283
(“………the viability of purified +IAA (82.6% ± 6.8) and –IAA (87.7% ± 4.0) RHTIR1-
VMP1AID tachyzoites was comparable, indicating that the decreased motility of +IAA
parasites is not associated with parasite viability.”).
Furthermore, the purified –IAA and +IAA parasites used for conoid extrusion, which
were obtained using the similar procedure, did not show any significant difference in conoid
extrusion (Supplementary Fig. 5). This data also ruled out differences in viability of purified –
IAA and +IAA parasites.
Comment 8. Some of the results deserve more discussion.
-Any explanation of why dense granules proteins but not rhoptry proteins accumulated at the
ER in the mutant ?
-VMP1 is an ER-resident protein so is expected to play a role in this compartment. Since the
three secretory organelles, micronemes, rhoptry and dense granules, transit through the ER,
why only dense granules and rhoptries are affected ? MICs proteins may follow, at some
level, a different trafficking pathway ?
-it is surprising to see that 50% of mice survived after infection with the mutant (+IAA) while
there is no plaques at all in vitro. The authors should comment on this discrepancy between
in vitro and in vivo.
Response: We agree with the reviewer’s points. This comments has 2 points, as suggested by
the reviewer, we have responded to these points below in a) and b).
a). “Any explanation of why dense granules proteins but not rhoptry proteins accumulated at
the ER………MICs proteins may follow, at some level, a different trafficking pathway ?”.
Response. We have discussed this point on page 32, line 794: “Different effects of TgVMP1
depletion on micronemes, rhoptries, and dense granules, could be due to differences in
the pathways leading to their biogenesis and secretion 3,4,6,49,67,68. It is possible that
TgVMP1 directly/indirectly regulates the proteins in ER/Golgi that are involved at
different stages of transport/maturation of the proteins destined to these organelles,
which is also supported by the presence of several proteins in TgVMP1 interactome that
regulate biogenesis of secretory organelles at different stages. Similar observations have
been reported earlier for TgSORTLR and V-type proton ATPase, which are required for
trafficking of microneme and rhoptry proteins 56,57, but not for dense granule proteins.
Similarly, depletion of apical annuli-associated proteins have been shown to have
different effects on dense granule secretion and plasma membrane proteins……..”.
b). it is surprising to see that 50% of mice survived after infection with the mutant (+IAA) while
there is no plaques at all in vitro. The authors should comment on this discrepancy between
in vitro and in vivo.
Response. We have discussed the difference in the effects of TgVMP1 depletion on in vitro
and in vivo parasite viability on page 9, line 224 (“This is in contrast to the complete block
of parasite development upon TgVMP1 depletion in plaque assay, which might be due to
differences in auxin bioavailability in in vitro and in vivo experimental settings.”).
Comment 9. The interpretation of mass spectrometry data are questionable. The authors
performed three independ IPs, but do not show any statistical significance of the enrichment,
that will help for the conclusions, especially because almost all the proteins that they used to
make their point are not enriched in the three sets of data. This is not clear how they connect
an association of VMP1 with these proteins (MICs, GRAs, ROPs, IMC proteins) and biogenesis
of secretory organelles.
Response: We thank the reviewer for bringing up this point to our notice. We reanalysed our
mass spectrometry data for statistically significant peptide enrichment in the TgVMP1AID
HA
immunoprecipitate compared to the control as mentioned in the Method section on page 53,
line 1463 (“….The peptide abundances in RHTIR1 and TgVMP1AID
HA
immunoprecipitates from 3 biological repeats were compared for enrichment analysis
using MetaboAnalyst 6.0 (https://www.metaboanalyst.ca/) with a single factor statistical
analysis. ……….Proteins enriched ≥1.5-fold with a P-value <0.05 in
TgVMP1AID immunoprecipitate compared to the RH-TIR1 immunoprecipitate were
HA
considered significant interactors of TgVMP1.”).
The revised supplementary Table 2 only contains proteins that are ≥ 1.5-fold enriched
with p-value ≤0.05 in TgVMP1 immunoprecipitate. The revised data contains multiple proteins
associated with micronemes, rhoptries, and dense granules (page 25, line 597: “….TgVMP1
interactome contained proteins that have been shown to localize to micronemes (apical
cap protein AC5 and MIC7), rhoptries (RON3, ROP8, ROP26, and ROP37), and dense
granules (phosphatidylserine decarboxylase, cathepsin CPC2, and
GRA12)…………gliding motility (PhiL1, GAPM3, GAPM2B, GAPM1A, and GRA12),
processing of the microneme and rhoptry proteins (V-type proton ATPase subunit a1),
and vesicle transport (sortilin-like receptor, Rab5b, glutathione S-transferase 2, and
Rab2)…...”).
Since the revised data also contains significantly enriched multiple organelle or
organelle-associated proteins, it is logical to propose that TgVMP1 may contribute to the
functioning and biogenesis of the secretory organelles via these proteins.
Comment 10. The authors referred to the absence of network when they look at IFA of dense
granule proteins. The IVN is not visible by IFA.
Response: We agree with the reviewer, and apologise for misinterpretation of the IFA data
(Fig. 6B, Supplementary Figure 8B). Indeed, IFA images showing diffuse GRA signal does
not indicate loss of IVN. We have revised the concerned result section and determined the
number of –IAA and +IAA PVs with IVN based on TEM micrographs on page 19, line 467
(“….The number of parasites with diffuse GRA1 or GRA2 localization was significantly
higher in +IAA parasites (83.6% for GRA1, 79.0% for GRA2) than that in –IAA parasites
(9.6% for GRA1, 14.6% for GRA2) (Fig. 6B; Supplementary Fig. 8B). TEM images
showed the absence of tubulo-vesicular IVN in the PV of 57.7% +IAA parasites (n=123
PVs) as compared with 7.8% –IAA parasites (n=64 PVs) (Fig. 6C), indicating a crucial
role for TgVMP1 in IVN formation.”).
Comment 11. Fig. S4A. For the fusion of miniAID in Plasmodium, did the authors control by
WB the expression of Tir1 in the transgenic line, which is a prerequisite for this conditional
KD ?
Response: This is a valid point. As suggested, we performed western blot of PfVMP1AID
parasites to check TIR1 expression using anti-TIR1 antibodies. We have discussed this point
in the text (page 8, line 189: “….. PfVMP1AID parasites expressed TIR1 (Supplementary
Fig. 3I), which ruled out failure of auxin-inducible knock-down due to its absence.”.
Comment 12. Section PfVMP1 and TgVMP1 localize to ER. ‘Towards characterization of
apicomplexan VMP1 proteins, we replaced wild-type PfVMP1 and TgVMP1 coding sequences
…’ This is not replacement of gene but endogenous tagging.
Response: We have rephrased this and other similar sentences on page 6, line 132 (“….the
endogenous PfVMP1 and TgVMP1 coding sequences in P. falciparum D10 and T. gondii
RHTIR1 strains were tagged in-frame at their 3’-ends with the coding sequences of GFP
and AID , respectively.”), page 8, line 178 (“…the endogenous PfVMP1 coding region
HA
was tagged in-frame at the 3’-end with cDDHA-glmS ribozyme coding sequence in P.
falciparum D10 strain to obtain a trimethoprim- and glucosamine-inducible conditional
knock-down line (PfVMP1dKD)…”), and page 8, line 182 (“..the endogenous PfVMP1
coding region was tagged in-frame with mAID -PcDT5U/TIR1-Flag-T2A/HD/PcDT3’U
HA
sequence in P. falciparum 3D7 strain to generate an auxin-inducible knock-down line
(PfVMP1AID)…”).
Comment 13. Figure S2 : Molecular sizes of PCR products on schematic and gels are missing.
Response: We thank the reviewer for such a detailed review and bringing up this point to our
notice. We have included molecular size markers and the sizes of expected PCR products in
Supplementary Fig. 3 and 4.
Comment 14. Table : add accession number TGGT1
Response: As suggested, we have included both Uniprot and ToxoDB IDs for each protein in
Supplementary Table 2.
References
Bisio, et al. The ZIP code of vesicle trafficking in Apicomplexa: SEC1/Munc18 and SNARE
proteins. MBio. 2020, 11(5), 10-1128.
Pelletier, L. et al. Golgi biogenesis in Toxoplasma gondii. Nature. 2002, 418, 548-552.
